## AI-generated Overview (from reference literature)

*This overview was drafted by an AI model from the cited scholarship and catalog data and may contain errors; verify against the sources before relying on it.*

The *Gijjhajātaka* (Ja 164) is a narrative in the Pali *Jātaka* collection. In the commentary's framing story set at Jetavana, the Buddha relates the tale regarding a monk who dutifully supported his mother (*mātuposakabhikkhu*), noting that the fuller background circumstances are related in the *Sāmajātaka* [Fausböll 1879].

In the story of the past (*atītavatthu*), set in Bārāṇasī during the reign of King Brahmadatta, the Bodhisatta was reborn as a vulture dwelling on Mount Gijjha (*Gijjhapabbata*) who supported his parents [Fausböll 1879]. During a tempest of rain and wind, cold and distressed vultures sought refuge by the moats and ramparts of Bārāṇasī, where a benevolent merchant of Bārāṇasī (*Bārāṇasīseṭṭhi*) provided them with shelter, warmth, and food [Fausböll 1879]. Subsequently, after articles taken from the city lead to the vulture's capture and appearance before the king, a verse exchange ensues regarding how a vulture capable of spotting a corpse from a hundred leagues away fails to perceive a hunter's snare when faculties wane or fate intervenes [Anandajoti 2010; Fausböll 1879]. Following the restoration of the goods, the vulture is freed [Fausböll 1879]. In the *samodhāna*, the Buddha identifies the king as Ānanda, the Bārāṇasī merchant as Sāriputta, and the filial vulture as the Bodhisatta [Fausböll 1879].
